JDK 27, where value classes became final
Only early-access builds of JDK 28, with --enable-preview
warmup.why: JEP 401 (value objects, preview) was integrated into the JDK mainline after JDK 27 had branched off, so it arrives in JDK 28, scheduled for March 2027; early-access builds have it now. JDK 25, 26 and 27 don't. Records are identity objects on every released JDK: == compares references, and you can synchronize on them.

sections.html:
Here is how a card issuer's reply often arrives in a service: one class, every field optional.

Java
public class IssuerReplyDto {
    String status;               // "APPROVED", "DECLINED" or "SOFT_DECLINE"
    String authCode;             // only when approved
    Long amountMinor;            // only when approved
    String declineCode;          // only when declined
    Long retryAfterSeconds;      // only on a soft decline
}
Kotlin
data class IssuerReplyDto(
    val status: String?,         // "APPROVED", "DECLINED" or "SOFT_DECLINE"
    val authCode: String?,       // only when approved
    val amountMinor: Long?,      // only when approved
    val declineCode: String?,    // only when declined
    val retryAfterSeconds: Long?,// only on a soft decline
)

Count what this type allows. Three statuses, times four optional fields that are each set or null, gives 48 shapes. Three of them make sense. The other 45, such as approved with no auth code, or approved with a decline code, can be built, serialized and passed around, and the comments are the only place that says which fields go together. Every consumer has to re-check that, and one of them won't: the capture job sends null as the auth code.

Model the three outcomes instead, each with only its own fields:

Java
public sealed interface AuthResult permits Approved, Declined, RetryLater {}
public record Approved(AuthCode code, long amountMinor) implements AuthResult {}
public record Declined(DeclineReason reason) implements AuthResult {}
public record RetryLater(Duration after) implements AuthResult {}
Kotlin
sealed interface AuthResult {
    data class Approved(val code: AuthCode, val amountMinor: Long) : AuthResult
    data class Declined(val reason: DeclineReason) : AuthResult
    data class RetryLater(val after: Duration) : AuthResult
}

Now there are three shapes, and "approved with a decline code" can't even be written down. The checks that are left move into the constructors: an AuthCode is six letters or digits, an approved amount is positive. That is what "make illegal states unrepresentable" means in practice. The types and the canonical constructors refuse the bad values once, so no consumer has to.

Brian Goetz calls this style data-oriented programming: model the data as immutable records and sealed types, and write the logic as functions over them. He wrote it up in a 2022 InfoQ article, "Data Oriented Programming in Java". His 2019 design note on records and sealed types gives the vocabulary. A record is a product type: an Approved is a code and an amount, and its API models "the state, the whole state, and nothing but the state". A sealed interface is a sum type, "a discriminated union of a fixed set of types": an AuthResult is approved or declined or retry-later. Most messages a payment service handles have exactly this shape: a few alternatives, each a fixed set of fields.

try.title: Count the shapes, then build a bad one
steps: Run IllegalStates (or IllegalStatesKt). Read the DTO consumer line: what will the capture job send to the issuer?
In the Java demo, try to build an Approved with a decline code. There is no constructor for it: the shape doesn't exist.
In the Kotlin twin, change AuthResult.Approved("", 4_200) to AuthResult.Approved(null, 4_200) and run. Which tool stopped you this time?

code.title: IllegalStates.java
code.html: package workbench.modernjava.l04.demo; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.Objects; /** One class with optional fields, against a sealed model that has only the valid shapes. */ public class IllegalStates { // the "bag of optionals" a JSON mapper gives you for the issuer's reply static final class IssuerReplyDto { final String status; // "APPROVED", "DECLINED" or "SOFT_DECLINE" final String authCode; // should be set only when approved final String declineCode; // should be set only when declined final Long retryAfterSeconds; // should be set only on a soft decline final Long amountMinor; // should be set only when approved IssuerReplyDto(String status, String authCode, String declineCode, Long retryAfterSeconds, Long amountMinor) { this.status = status; this.authCode = authCode; this.declineCode = declineCode; this.retryAfterSeconds = retryAfterSeconds; this.amountMinor = amountMinor; } } // a consumer of the DTO: it trusts that the fields match the status static String captureCommand(IssuerReplyDto r) { if ("APPROVED".equals(r.status)) return "capture " + r.amountMinor + " with auth code " + r.authCode; return "no capture"; } // the same information as a closed model: three shapes, each with only its own fields sealed interface AuthResult permits Approved, Declined, RetryLater {} record Approved(String authCode, long amountMinor) implements AuthResult { Approved { Objects.requireNonNull(authCode, "authCode"); if (amountMinor <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("amount must be positive"); } } record Declined(String declineCode) implements AuthResult {} record RetryLater(Duration after) implements AuthResult {} static String captureCommand(AuthResult r) { return switch (r) { case Approved(var code, var amount) -> "capture " + amount + " with auth code " + code; case Declined d -> "no capture"; case RetryLater later -> "no capture yet"; }; } public static void main(String[] args) { int statuses = 3, optionalFields = 4; System.out.println("shapes the DTO allows: " + statuses * (1 << optionalFields) + ", shapes that make sense: 3"); // approved, but with no auth code and a decline code: nothing stops it IssuerReplyDto broken = new IssuerReplyDto("APPROVED", null, "51", null, 4_200L); System.out.println("DTO consumer: " + captureCommand(broken)); try { new Approved(null, 4_200); } catch (NullPointerException e) { System.out.println("sealed model: refused, " + e.getMessage() + " is required"); } System.out.println("sealed consumer: " + captureCommand(new Approved("A1B2C3", 4_200))); } }

init { require(authCode.isNotBlank()) { "authCode is required" } require(amountMinor > 0) { "amount must be positive" } } } data class Declined(val declineCode: String?) : AuthResult data class RetryLater(val after: Duration) : AuthResult } fun captureCommand(r: AuthResult): String = when (r) { is AuthResult.Approved -> "capture ${r.amountMinor} with auth code ${r.authCode}" is AuthResult.Declined -> "no capture" is AuthResult.RetryLater -> "no capture yet" } /** One class with optional fields, against a sealed model that has only the valid shapes. */ fun main() { val statuses = 3 val optionalFields = 4 println("shapes the DTO allows: ${statuses * (1 shl optionalFields)}, shapes that make sense: 3") // approved, but with no auth code and a decline code: nothing stops it val broken = IssuerReplyDto("APPROVED", null, "51", null, 4_200) println("DTO consumer: ${captureCommand(broken)}") // AuthResult.Approved(null, 4_200) doesn't even compile: the type says the code is there try { AuthResult.Approved("", 4_200) } catch (e: IllegalArgumentException) { println("sealed model: refused, ${e.message}") } println("sealed consumer: ${captureCommand(AuthResult.Approved("A1B2C3", 4_200))}") }

try.expect: Both print shapes the DTO allows: 48, shapes that make sense: 3, then DTO consumer: capture 4200 with auth code null: nothing stopped an approved reply with no code. The sealed model refuses it (authCode is required) and the valid approval prints capture 4200 with auth code A1B2C3. In Kotlin, Approved(null, 4_200) doesn't compile at all, because the property is a non-null String: the type system did the constructor's job.

sections.h: Parse at the edge, then trust the types
sections.html:
The sealed model only helps if untrusted data can't get in around it. So the service converts raw input into the model in exactly one place, at its edge: the REST resource, the Kafka deserializer, the client for the issuer's API. Everything behind the edge works only with model values.

Java
static Parsed parse(IssuerReplyDto raw) {
    try {
        return switch (raw.status) {
            case "APPROVED" -> raw.authCode == null || raw.amountMinor == null
                    ? new Rejected("approved without a code or an amount")
                    : new Ok(new Approved(new AuthCode(raw.authCode), raw.amountMinor));
            case "DECLINED" -> new Ok(new Declined(DeclineReason.fromCode(raw.declineCode)));
            case "SOFT_DECLINE" -> raw.retryAfterSeconds == null
                    ? new Rejected("soft decline without retry-after")
                    : new Ok(new RetryLater(Duration.ofSeconds(raw.retryAfterSeconds)));
            case null, default -> new Rejected("unknown status: " + raw.status);
        };
    } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
        return new Rejected(e.getMessage());          // a constructor refused a value
    }
}
Kotlin
fun parse(raw: IssuerReplyDto): Parsed = try {
    when (raw.status) {
        "APPROVED" ->
            if (raw.authCode == null || raw.amountMinor == null) Rejected("approved without a code or an amount")
            else Ok(Approved(AuthCode(raw.authCode), raw.amountMinor))
        "DECLINED" -> Ok(Declined(DeclineReason.fromCode(raw.declineCode)))
        "SOFT_DECLINE" ->
            if (raw.retryAfterSeconds == null) Rejected("soft decline without retry-after")
            else Ok(RetryLater(Duration.ofSeconds(raw.retryAfterSeconds)))
        else -> Rejected("unknown status: ${raw.status}")
    }
} catch (e: IllegalArgumentException) {
    Rejected(e.message ?: "invalid reply")            // a constructor refused a value
}

Two details make this work. The function never throws. A reply the model refuses comes back as Rejected with a reason, and the caller decides what that means (log it, alert, fail the payment safely) instead of an exception escaping from somewhere inside a mapper. And the constructors stay the final check: parse doesn't repeat the auth-code rule, it calls new AuthCode(...) and turns the refusal into a Rejected.

Behind the edge, nothing re-validates. A method that takes an Approved knows it has a valid code and a positive amount, because no other kind of Approved can exist. Records, data classes and sealed types make this cheap: the model is a dozen lines, the edge is one function, and the compiler checks every switch in between. The lab builds exactly this for the issuer reply, in Kotlin, including the case the snippets above skip: an approved reply that also carries a decline code contradicts itself, and must be rejected.

try.title: Predict what the edge does
steps: The issuer sends status: "APPROVED " (with a trailing space), auth code A1B2C3 and amount 4200. Which arm of parse takes it, and what does the capture job see?
It sends a soft decline with retryAfterSeconds: 0. Does parse or a constructor produce the result?
A teammate adds if (approved.amountMinor() <= 0) return; inside the capture job. Can that line ever run?
try.expect: The trailing space matches no status string, so case null, default returns Rejected("unknown status: APPROVED ") and the capture job never sees the reply: a strict edge turns a sloppy reply into a visible rejection instead of a capture with bad data. The zero wait gets past parse, because the field isn't null, and is refused by the RetryLater constructor once it has the range check (as the lab's does); the catch turns that refusal into Rejected. The teammate's line is dead code: an Approved with a non-positive amount can't be built, so the check can never be true.

sections.html:
In classic object-oriented design, behavior lives in the classes: result.customerMessage(), result.nextStep(), result.metricTag(), each written three times across Approved, Declined and RetryLater. Data-oriented code keeps the records plain and writes each operation as one function with a switch:

Java
static String customerMessage(AuthResult r) {
    return switch (r) {
        case Approved a -> "Payment approved.";
        case Declined(var reason) when reason == DeclineReason.INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS -> "Not enough funds. Try another card.";
        case Declined d -> "Payment declined.";
        case RetryLater(var after) -> "Your bank is busy. We'll try again in " + after.toSeconds() + " seconds.";
    };
}
Kotlin
fun customerMessage(r: AuthResult): String = when (r) {
    is Approved -> "Payment approved."
    is Declined if r.reason == DeclineReason.INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS -> "Not enough funds. Try another card."
    is Declined -> "Payment declined."
    is RetryLater -> "Your bank is busy. We'll try again in ${r.after.seconds} seconds."
}

Everything about customer messages sits in one function, the records don't depend on your translation code, and the next operation (a metrics tag, a ledger posting) is a new function that touches nothing else.

That is one side of the expression problem, which Visitor, Iterator, Mediator and Memento in the patterns track introduced. With methods on the classes, adding a type is local and adding an operation means editing every class. With sealed types and switches it is the other way round: a new operation is one function, and a new type breaks every switch until you handle it. Neither style makes both changes cheap, so choose by the change you expect more often.

For payment data (authorization results, events, ledger entries, scheme messages) the set of types changes rarely and new operations keep arriving, so the data-oriented side wins. For open hierarchies that other teams extend, such as fraud checks or the PartnerMethod branch from lesson 2, keep an interface with methods. And behavior that is about the value itself, like Money.plus, belongs on the record. Keep business decisions out of the records; small methods that compute with the value itself can stay.

try.title: Pay both costs
steps: Write operation 3 where the comment says: isCustomerFacing, true for charges and refunds, false for fees. How many existing lines did you change?
Add the Chargeback record (in Java, add it to permits too) and run. List the places the compiler asks you to change.
Decide what a chargeback does to the balance and to the statement line, and handle it in each function.

code.title: ExpressionProblem.java
code.html: package workbench.modernjava.l04.demo; import java.util.List; /** Data in records, operations in functions. Add an operation, then add a type, and compare the cost. */ public class ExpressionProblem { sealed interface LedgerEntry permits Charge, Refund, Fee {} record Charge(String paymentId, long amountMinor) implements LedgerEntry {} record Refund(String paymentId, long amountMinor) implements LedgerEntry {} record Fee(String reason, long amountMinor) implements LedgerEntry {} // Step 3: add Chargeback to the permits clause, then uncomment this record. // record Chargeback(String paymentId, long amountMinor, String caseId) implements LedgerEntry {} // operation 1: how the entry moves the merchant's balance static long balanceDelta(LedgerEntry e) { return switch (e) { case Charge c -> c.amountMinor(); case Refund r -> -r.amountMinor(); case Fee f -> -f.amountMinor(); }; } // operation 2: the line on the merchant's statement static String statementLine(LedgerEntry e) { return switch (e) { case Charge(var id, var amt) -> "payment " + id + " +" + amt; case Refund(var id, var amt) -> "refund " + id + " -" + amt; case Fee(var reason, var amt) -> "fee " + reason + " -" + amt; }; } // Step 2: write operation 3 here, isCustomerFacing(LedgerEntry), as one more switch. public static void main(String[] args) { List<LedgerEntry> day = List.of(new Charge("pay_1", 10_000), new Fee("scheme fee", 35), new Refund("pay_1", 2_500)); long balance = 0; for (LedgerEntry e : day) { balance += balanceDelta(e); System.out.println(statementLine(e)); } System.out.println("balance " + balance); } }

Add an operation, then add a type, and compare the cost. */ fun main() { val day = listOf(LedgerEntry.Charge("pay_1", 10_000), LedgerEntry.Fee("scheme fee", 35), LedgerEntry.Refund("pay_1", 2_500)) var balance = 0L for (e in day) { balance += balanceDelta(e) println(statementLine(e)) } println("balance $balance") }

try.expect: The demo prints three statement lines and balance 7465. Adding isCustomerFacing changed no existing line. Adding Chargeback makes javac report each switch over LedgerEntry (balanceDelta, statementLine and your new one) with does not cover all possible input values, and kotlinc asks for the 'is Chargeback' branch in each when. A new operation cost one function; a new type cost one edit per operation, and the compiler found every one.

sections.html:
Records are identity objects, and lesson 1 showed what that means. == compares references, you can lock on a record, and an array of Money is an array of references to separate heap objects. Project Valhalla's first feature lets a class give up identity:

Java
value record Money(long minor, String currency) {}   // JDK 28 early-access builds, --enable-preview
Kotlin
@JvmInline
value class AuthCode(val value: String)               // Kotlin today: one property, compiled away

The status is often misreported, so here it is precisely. JEP 401, Value Objects (Preview), together with JEP 539 (strict field initialization in the JVM), was integrated into the JDK mainline on 31 July 2026. JDK 27 had already branched off, so the feature ships in JDK 28, scheduled for 23 March 2027, and early-access builds of JDK 28 exist now. It is a preview: it needs --enable-preview and can still change. JDK 25, 26 and 27 don't have it.

The Valhalla docs define value objects as immutable objects that lack identity, "distinguished solely by the values of their fields". == compares two value objects by their state, and identity operations such as synchronization fail with an exception. In return, the JVM may store them flat. In JDK 28 that means two optimizations. Flattening stores a value's fields directly inside the field or array element that holds it, with no separate object and no pointer. Scalarization lets JIT-compiled code keep the fields in registers and skip the allocation. Both have limits the docs spell out. Flattened values are read and written atomically and must allow null, so value objects with 64 bits or more of field data "cannot normally be flattened". Scalarization only happens once C2, the JIT's optimizing compiler, has compiled the code. Polymorphic variables, including those in generic APIs, aren't flattened. By the first rule, the Money above would not normally be flattened, since its long alone is 64 bits. Small records of a few int or short fields gain first.

With the preview on, 28 JDK classes become value classes, among them Integer, Long, Optional, LocalDate, Instant and Duration. Synchronizing on an Integer, or putting one in a WeakReference, then throws IdentityException. Null-restricted types, the other thing people expect from Valhalla, are still draft JEPs.

Kotlin's @JvmInline value class is an older, different trick. It holds one property and is erased to that property where the compiler can: a function taking an AuthCode compiles to one taking a String, under a mangled name. It is boxed when used as a generic T, an interface or a nullable type. Kotlin's design notes say the annotation leaves room for real Valhalla value classes later, but no such mode has shipped, so a Kotlin data class on JDK 28 is still an identity object.

What to do today: don't depend on the identity of your records. No == between them, no synchronized on them, no identity-keyed maps. Then adopting value later is a one-word change.

try.title: Look at identity, then at a Kotlin value class
steps: Run IdentityDemo. Which of its lines would change if Money were a value record?
From labs/, run javap -p modernjava/build/classes/kotlin/demo/workbench/modernjava/l04/demo/IdentityDemoKt.class. What parameter type does describeIban take?

code.title: IdentityDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.modernjava.l04.demo; /** Records are identity objects today. Here is what that identity looks like. */ public class IdentityDemo { record Money(long minor, String currency) {} public static void main(String[] args) { Money a = new Money(4_200, "EUR"); Money b = new Money(4_200, "EUR"); System.out.println("equals: " + a.equals(b) + ", ==: " + (a == b)); System.out.println("identity hash codes differ: " + (System.identityHashCode(a) != System.identityHashCode(b))); synchronized (a) { System.out.println("synchronized on a record: allowed, because it has an identity"); } // the Integer box cache lets identity leak into == for some values and not others Integer x = 127, y = 127, p = 128, q = 128; System.out.println("Integer 127 == 127: " + (x == y) + ", 128 == 128: " + (p == q)); // an array of records is an array of references to separate heap objects Money[] ledger = { a, b, a }; System.out.println("ledger[0] == ledger[2]: " + (ledger[0] == ledger[2]) + ", ledger[0] == ledger[1]: " + (ledger[0] == ledger[1])); } }

alt.title: IdentityDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.modernjava.l04.demo data class MoneyAmount(val minor: Long, val currency: String) // Kotlin's value class today: one property, erased to that property wherever the compiler can @JvmInline value class Iban(val value: String) fun describeIban(iban: Iban): String = "IBAN ending ${iban.value.takeLast(4)}" /** Data classes are identity objects today; @JvmInline value classes are a compile-time trick. */ fun main() { val a = MoneyAmount(4_200, "EUR") val b = MoneyAmount(4_200, "EUR") println("==: ${a == b}, ===: ${a === b}") synchronized(a) { println("synchronized on a data class: allowed, because it has an identity") } val iban = Iban("DE89370400440532013000") println(describeIban(iban)) // compiled to a call taking a plain String val asAny: Any = iban // used as another type: boxed println("as Any, the object is a ${asAny::class.java.simpleName}") val inList = listOf(iban) // used as a generic T: boxed println("in a List, the element is a ${(inList[0] as Any)::class.java.simpleName}") }

try.expect: equals: true, ==: false, different identity hash codes, a successful synchronized, Integer 127 == 127: true, 128 == 128: false, and ledger[0] == ledger[2]: true, ledger[0] == ledger[1]: false. With a value record, == would compare state, so a == b and ledger[0] == ledger[1] would be true, and synchronized would be refused. In Kotlin, javap shows describeIban-JSx-I4w(java.lang.String): the value class is erased to a String under a mangled name, and the demo shows it boxed back into an Iban when stored as Any or in a List.

analogy: Data-oriented code works like a payment network's message specification. A message is just fields with fixed meanings, the spec says which fields each message type carries, and every processor that reads the messages keeps its own logic (routing, risk, settlement) in its own system. Nobody ships behavior inside the message. A new processing step is easy to add, while a new message type means every processor updates its handling. The analogy breaks on enforcement: a spec is a document that a sender can violate, while a sealed type with validating constructors makes the bad message impossible to build in the first place.
world: Look at the DTOs your Quarkus REST clients and Kafka consumers map into. Many are one class per endpoint, with a status field and a dozen nullable fields, and the rules about which fields go together live in if statements spread across services. Pick the one that causes the most defensive code (usually the issuer or acquirer response) and put a sealed model behind it. The DTO stays at the edge, where your JSON mapper keeps filling it. One parse function turns it into the model. Everything downstream, from the capture job to the retry scheduler to the Temporal workflow waiting for a soft decline to clear, switches over three records instead of re-checking strings. Valhalla needs nothing from you yet: keep your records free of identity tricks, and look again when JDK 28 is final and your frameworks support it.
mistake: The common mistake is building the sealed model and then sneaking the old states back in: a shared details record with nullable fields inside each outcome, or a status enum stored next to the sealed type "for convenience". Now a Declined can carry status = APPROVED, and every consumer has to wonder which one is true. If two facts must agree, derive one from the other (a method computed from the type) or delete it. The opposite mistake is sealing an extension point, such as the interface partner teams implement, to get exhaustive switches; then every new partner needs a change in your module. Seal closed domains and leave plug-in points open.

compare.title: One model and one operation in Java and Kotlin

java.title: AuthResult.java
java.html: public record AuthCode(String value) { public AuthCode { if (value == null || !value.matches("[A-Z0-9]{6}")) throw new IllegalArgumentException("bad auth code"); } } public sealed interface AuthResult permits Approved, Declined, RetryLater {} public record Approved(AuthCode code, long amountMinor) implements AuthResult { public Approved { if (amountMinor <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("amount must be positive"); } } public record Declined(DeclineReason reason) implements AuthResult {} public record RetryLater(Duration after) implements AuthResult {} static String customerMessage(AuthResult r) { return switch (r) { case Approved a -> "Payment approved."; case Declined(var reason) when reason == DeclineReason.SUSPECTED_FRAUD -> "Payment declined. Please contact your bank."; case Declined d -> "Payment declined."; case RetryLater(var after) -> "Your bank is busy. We'll try again in " + after.toSeconds() + " seconds."; }; }

kotlin.title: AuthResult.kt
kotlin.html: @JvmInline value class AuthCode(val value: String) { init { require(value.matches(Regex("[A-Z0-9]{6}"))) { "bad auth code" } } } sealed interface AuthResult { data class Approved(val code: AuthCode, val amountMinor: Long) : AuthResult { init { require(amountMinor > 0) { "amount must be positive" } } } data class Declined(val reason: DeclineReason) : AuthResult data class RetryLater(val after: Duration) : AuthResult } fun customerMessage(r: AuthResult): String = when (r) { is AuthResult.Approved -> "Payment approved." is AuthResult.Declined if r.reason == DeclineReason.SUSPECTED_FRAUD -> "Payment declined. Please contact your bank." is AuthResult.Declined -> "Payment declined." is AuthResult.RetryLater -> "Your bank is busy. We'll try again in ${r.after.seconds} seconds." }

compare.note: The design is identical: a closed set of outcomes, each with only its own fields, constructors that refuse bad values, and an operation written as one exhaustive switch outside the data. Two things differ. Java's switch takes Declined apart in the label (Declined(var reason)), while Kotlin tests the type and reads r.reason after a smart cast. And AuthCode is a record in Java, which is a full object with identity, while Kotlin's @JvmInline value class is usually erased to a plain String. With JDK 28's preview, Java could write value record AuthCode(String value) and give up identity at the JVM level, which is something Kotlin's value class doesn't do today.

worked.title: From a payout webhook DTO to a closed model

steps.say: A payout provider calls your webhook with this body. Its docs say: a PAID event has an arrival date, a FAILED event has a reason, and a RETURNED event has the returned amount. The DTO encodes none of that.
steps.code: public record PayoutWebhookDto(String type, String payoutId, LocalDate arrivalDate, String failureReason, Long returnedMinor) {}

alt.html: data class PayoutWebhookDto(val type: String?, val payoutId: String?, val arrivalDate: LocalDate?, val failureReason: String?, val returnedMinor: Long?)

steps.say: Write one record per row of the provider's docs. Every field is required, so the record can't be half a PAID event.
steps.code: // 1. one record per valid combination public sealed interface PayoutEvent permits Paid, PayoutFailed, Returned {} public record Paid(String payoutId, LocalDate arrivalDate) implements PayoutEvent {} public record PayoutFailed(String payoutId, String reason) implements PayoutEvent {} public record Returned(String payoutId, long amountMinor) implements PayoutEvent { public Returned { if (amountMinor <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("returned amount must be positive"); } }

alt.html: // 1. one class per valid combination, with non-null properties sealed interface PayoutEvent { data class Paid(val payoutId: String, val arrivalDate: LocalDate) : PayoutEvent data class Failed(val payoutId: String, val reason: String) : PayoutEvent data class Returned(val payoutId: String, val amountMinor: Long) : PayoutEvent { init { require(amountMinor > 0) { "returned amount must be positive" } } } }

steps.say: Write the edge. It is the only code that looks at the DTO, and it checks that each type carries its own field. A null where the docs promise a value becomes a clear error here, not a NullPointerException three services later.
steps.code: // 2. the edge: DTO in, model out static PayoutEvent toEvent(PayoutWebhookDto d) { Objects.requireNonNull(d.payoutId(), "payoutId"); return switch (d.type()) { case "PAID" -> new Paid(d.payoutId(), Objects.requireNonNull(d.arrivalDate(), "arrivalDate")); case "FAILED" -> new PayoutFailed(d.payoutId(), Objects.requireNonNull(d.failureReason(), "failureReason")); case "RETURNED" -> new Returned(d.payoutId(), Objects.requireNonNull(d.returnedMinor(), "returnedMinor")); case null, default -> throw new IllegalArgumentException("unknown payout event: " + d.type()); }; }

alt.html: // 2. the edge: DTO in, model out fun toEvent(d: PayoutWebhookDto): PayoutEvent { val id = requireNotNull(d.payoutId) { "payoutId" } return when (d.type) { "PAID" -> PayoutEvent.Paid(id, requireNotNull(d.arrivalDate) { "arrivalDate" }) "FAILED" -> PayoutEvent.Failed(id, requireNotNull(d.failureReason) { "failureReason" }) "RETURNED" -> PayoutEvent.Returned(id, requireNotNull(d.returnedMinor) { "returnedMinor" }) else -> throw IllegalArgumentException("unknown payout event: ${d.type}") } }

steps.say: Now the consumer. The old one was thirty lines of if ("PAID".equals(type) && arrivalDate != null). The new one is a switch with no default, so a new event type from the provider shows up as a compile error, not a silently ignored webhook.
steps.code: // 3. behind the edge: trust the types static void apply(PayoutEvent e, Ledger ledger) { switch (e) { case Paid(var id, var date) -> ledger.markSettled(id, date); case PayoutFailed(var id, var reason) -> ledger.reopen(id, reason); case Returned(var id, long amount) -> ledger.credit(id, amount); } }

alt.html: // 3. behind the edge: trust the types fun apply(e: PayoutEvent, ledger: Ledger) = when (e) { is PayoutEvent.Paid -> ledger.markSettled(e.payoutId, e.arrivalDate) is PayoutEvent.Failed -> ledger.reopen(e.payoutId, e.reason) is PayoutEvent.Returned -> ledger.credit(e.payoutId, e.amountMinor) }

lab.title: Parse an issuer reply into a model with no illegal states
steps: Run the tests: all ten fail. This lab is in Kotlin. The model is in AuthModel.kt and the boundary and the operation are in IssuerReplies.kt.
Make the model refuse what can't be real: write the init checks in AuthCode, Approved and RetryLater (TODO 1 to 3). Three tests should pass now.
Write parse (TODO 4) as one when on the status. Let the constructors do their own checks, and turn their IllegalArgumentException into Rejected.
Write customerMessage (TODO 5) as one when with guards and no else.

When all ten pass, add data class PartialApproval(val code: AuthCode, val approvedMinor: Long) : AuthResult to the model and run ./gradlew :modernjava:compileKotlin. Which function does kotlinc point at? Remove it again.
hints: A value class may have an init block: init { require(Regex("[A-Z0-9]{6}").matches(value)) { "bad auth code: $value" } }.
Duration is Comparable, so after >= Duration.ofSeconds(1) && after <= Duration.ofHours(1) works in Kotlin.
Wrap the whole when in try { ... } catch (e: IllegalArgumentException) { Rejected(e.message ?: "invalid reply") }. Duration.ofSeconds(0) is fine; it is RetryLater that refuses it.
After a branch like raw.authCode == null -> Rejected(...), Kotlin smart-casts raw.authCode to String in the later branches, because it is a val of a class in the same module.
A guard looks like is Declined if result.reason == DeclineReason.SUSPECTED_FRAUD -> ....

drill.title: Model a webhook from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. A refund webhook has a type ("SUCCEEDED", "FAILED" or "PENDING"), a refundId, and a failureCode that is present only when the refund failed. Write the sealed model in Java so that a failure can't lack its code, and a parse(type, refundId, failureCode) that throws IllegalArgumentException for an unknown or missing type. Then write the Kotlin version.

answer.html: sealed interface RefundEvent permits Succeeded, Failed, Pending {} record Succeeded(String refundId) implements RefundEvent {} record Failed(String refundId, String failureCode) implements RefundEvent { Failed { Objects.requireNonNull(failureCode, "failureCode"); } // a failure always has a code } record Pending(String refundId) implements RefundEvent {} static RefundEvent parse(String type, String refundId, String failureCode) { return switch (type) { case "SUCCEEDED" -> new Succeeded(refundId); case "FAILED" -> new Failed(refundId, failureCode); case "PENDING" -> new Pending(refundId); case null, default -> throw new IllegalArgumentException("unknown refund event: " + type); }; }

alt.html: sealed interface RefundEvent { data class Succeeded(val refundId: String) : RefundEvent data class Failed(val refundId: String, val failureCode: String) : RefundEvent // non-null: always has a code data class Pending(val refundId: String) : RefundEvent } fun parse(type: String?, refundId: String, failureCode: String?): RefundEvent = when (type) { "SUCCEEDED" -> RefundEvent.Succeeded(refundId) "FAILED" -> RefundEvent.Failed(refundId, requireNotNull(failureCode) { "failureCode" }) "PENDING" -> RefundEvent.Pending(refundId) else -> throw IllegalArgumentException("unknown refund event: $type") }

recap: Model each valid combination as its own record under a sealed interface, and check values in the constructors. A shape that can't be written down can't reach your code.
Records are product types (this and that) and sealed interfaces are sum types (this or that). Most payment messages are a few alternatives, each a fixed set of fields.
Parse untrusted input into the model once, at the edge, and return a result instead of throwing. Behind the edge, trust the types.
Write business operations as functions that switch over the data. A new operation is one function; a new type breaks every switch, and the compiler lists them.
Keep interfaces with methods for open hierarchies that others extend, and keep methods about the value itself on the record.
Valhalla's value objects are a preview feature of JDK 28, not of 25, 26 or 27. Records are identity objects, so don't depend on their identity.

explain.prompt: Your team lead asks: "Should we move our payment model to records and sealed types now, or wait for Valhalla to make it fast?" Answer in your own words: what the data-oriented style gives you today, where you would and wouldn't use it, and what Valhalla changes.
explain.answer: The data-oriented style pays off today, with no new JDK: records and sealed types are final since JDK 17, and pattern switches since 21. Modeling each valid outcome as its own record means contradictory states can't be built, parsing at the edge means only valid values get in, and exhaustive switches mean the compiler tells us every place to update when a type is added. I'd use it for closed domain data such as authorization results, payment events and ledger entries, and keep ordinary interfaces for things other teams extend, like fraud checks. Valhalla changes performance and identity; it doesn't change this design. JEP 401 is only a preview in JDK 28, and even there, records like Money with a long and a reference wouldn't normally be flattened. So we shouldn't wait for it; we should just avoid depending on record identity, so that adding value later is easy.

deeper.html:
Brian Goetz's January 2026 design note, "Data-Oriented Programming for Java: Beyond Records", says where Amber goes next. It calls records, sealed classes and record patterns "the first feature arc of 'data-oriented programming' for Java", and announces the next arc: carrier classes and carrier interfaces. A carrier class is a normal class with a record-style state description in its header. It would declare its own fields and need not be final, yet still have a canonical constructor, accessors and a deconstruction pattern, so data that is almost a record (one cached field, one derived value) doesn't force you back to writing everything by hand.

The note also describes reconstruction, the with expression from JEP 468, and points out how much its block resembles a compact constructor body: the component variables start with the old values, your block changes some of them, and the canonical constructor builds the new value, so the invariants still hold. Goetz explains that JEP 468 has been "on hold" until there was a path to extend it beyond records. The note also mentions an upcoming pattern assignment statement, for taking a record apart in an ordinary assignment.

None of this is in a JDK or a JEP you can use. The design direction is useful anyway: it says the language will keep making "model the data with records and sealed types, switch over it" cheaper, so code written in that style today is code the platform is moving toward.

On the Valhalla side, the next pieces on the project page are null-restricted storage, array enhancements, unifying primitives with classes, and a parametric JVM that can specialize generics. Only the first piece, value objects, has a JEP that has been integrated, and it is a preview.
